translation:
"Seek first God's kingdom, and all these things will be added to you." —LUKE 12:31.
NOTES: 40, 44
1. Why is it that people worry about such things as food and clothing when a person dies and leaves them behind?
People have great possessions, yet they often worry about getting enough food. It seems that many people worry about such things as food and clothing even though they have plenty. What causes this worrying? The reason is that they do not value what they have and think they need more. Some things that people worry about are trivial, like clothes, shoes, and hairstyles. Worrying about such things, and many other things, makes a person unhappy unless he is satisfied with what he has.
2. What prevents people from being happy?
Many people are unhappy because they compare themselves with others who have more than they do. Many people feel dissatisfied because they always want something better—a bigger house, a newer car, or fancier furniture. Others feel dissatisfied because they want more power and influence, to own a larger business, or to have more money. But even if someone feels dissatisfied, the main reason is usually this: He does not appreciate what he has, whether it is his health, his family, or his friends, or whether he has food or clothing, or whether he has a home or not.
LET US BE CONTENT WITH WHAT WE HAVE
3. How can a person be content?
3 How can a person be content? A person who appreciates what he has each day will not constantly yearn for things he does not have. Such a person will also be less likely to become greedy or envious. Being content helps us to focus on important things. It prevents us from wasting time worrying about things we do not have.
However, some with many possessions still find it difficult to be content, and they may envy those who seem to have more. They may use their possessions to try to impress others.—Prov. 13:5.
4. Does Satan tempt people with "the desire for things"?
4 Satan uses materialism to mislead us into thinking that we need certain things to be happy, or that we deserve them. He wants us to feel dissatisfied with what we have and to crave more. This is how he promotes "the desire for things." (1 John 2:15-17; Gen. 3:6; Prov. 27:20) Materialism can distract us from spiritual pursuits, and it can lead to unwise decisions. Are you easily influenced by advertising or do you often compare yourself with others? Do you feel that you need expensive items to be accepted? Is it wise to risk getting into debt just to have something you want? The desire for things can blind us and make us selfish. It can cause us to neglect our Bible study, our meetings, our ministry, and our relationships, and it can prevent us from being grateful. As the apostle John wrote: "The world and its desires pass away."—1 John 2:17.
5. Do people who spend much time acquiring possessions ever become content?
5 Satan tries to turn people against Jehovah. (Matt. 6:24) But those who focus on accumulating possessions often find themselves stressed and anxious because they worry about losing what they have. And even if they succeed in gaining wealth, it may not bring them lasting joy or strengthen their relationship with Jehovah. (1 Tim. 6:9, 10; Eccl. 3:17) Many things that Jesus warned about were like weeds sown among wheat. That seed "produces fruit, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, and some a hundredfold."—Mark 4:14, 18, 19.
6. What does the parable of the talents illustrate?
6 Let us examine the parable of the slave whom Jeremiah appointed as manager. When Jerusalem was about to be conquered, this slave told his master, "I will go out and become a traveling merchant." He used his position to get rich quickly. However, he did not use his resources to help others, and Jehovah said to him: "Look! I am going to bring disaster upon you." (Jer. 45:1-5) God can see a person's motives and knows when someone is using his position selfishly. (Jer. 20:5) So we should be careful not to misuse our privileges, and we should not try to profit from difficult times. We also need to remember that we may lose everything we have gained, and we should not become overly attached to material things.—Prov. 11:4; Matt. 24:21, 22; Luke 12:15.
7. What will we discuss now, and why?
7 Jesus taught us the importance of not being overly anxious about material possessions, fearing financial ruin, or becoming obsessed with getting ahead. He illustrated this with the parable of the Rich Man. (Matt. 6:19-21) Let us read and discuss Matthew 6:25-34. This will help us understand how to avoid 'worrying about life' unnecessarily.—Luke 12:31.
JEHOVAH PROVIDES FOR OUR NEEDS
8, 9. (a) How can we show that we trust in God's provision? (b) How did Jesus view riches and possessions?
8 Read Matthew 6:25. Jesus knew his disciples were concerned about "what they would eat" and "what they would wear." He encouraged them not to be unduly anxious. It is vital to focus on what is truly important. Jesus showed that he valued spiritual things above material possessions. To worry about getting ahead or to become preoccupied with accumulating wealth is to allow oneself to be distracted from serving Jehovah wholeheartedly. It can lead to dissatisfaction and unhappiness. Jesus was willing to give up comfort and endure hardship because he trusted that his Father would provide for him.—Matt. 6:27, 28, 31, 34.
9 Does Jesus expect us to stop working, stop eating, or stop dressing ourselves? Of course not! Such thinking would be impractical. They asked him if this was true! We can trust that God will supply our needs, so we should not be overly anxious. And Jesus assures us that God will supply our needs, just as he does for the birds and the lilies—creatures that do not store up provisions for the future. Also, he assures us that he cares for his faithful servants who face difficulties and trials, such as those described as "difficult times" and "distressing times." (2 Tim. 3:1) These include war, famine, pestilence, and great earthquakes. So despite everything, Jesus encourages us to say, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we wear?"
10. But did Jesus tell his followers to be lazy, or was there something else he wanted them to understand about being anxious?
10 Jesus told his disciples to pray for God's Kingdom, and he taught them how to ask for daily bread. He encouraged them to pray: "Give us today the bread for tomorrow." (Matt. 6:11) And although he gave them a simple example, the principle applies to all our needs: "Give us each day the bread for tomorrow." (Luke 11:3) Thus, by praying regularly, we show that we rely on God to provide what we need. By means of prayer, Jesus showed his Father's will, and whatever we ask for in harmony with that will is an expression of reverence for Jehovah's name. (Matt. 6:10; Luke 11:2) And because he knows what is best for us, he will fulfill his purpose.
11, 12. What can we learn from the way Jehovah answers prayers? (See accompanying article, "How to Make Your Prayers Effective.")
11 Read Matthew 6:26. Jesus said: "Observe carefully the birds of heaven." We can learn much from observing how they diligently seek food, and we can apply this lesson to our own lives. Just as birds work hard to find food, so too should we put effort into meeting our needs. But instead of worrying about whether we will have enough, we trust that Jehovah will care for us. (Ps. 147:9) So let us not be anxious about tomorrow, but let us confidently look to Jehovah for help. If we do, we will be more inclined to focus on spiritual things and less on material concerns.
12 Jesus knew that his Father wanted people to use their resources wisely and to appreciate the value of what they had. [1] (1 Pet. 5:6, 7) Let us therefore be diligent in managing our possessions, being determined to use them to honor Jehovah and to support his worship. And let us also remember that we can show appreciation for what we have by using it to help others. Moreover, the blessings we receive motivate us to be grateful and to continue serving Jehovah faithfully. And like Jesus demonstrated, Jehovah wants us to be generous, Jehovah equips us with the wisdom and discernment needed to make practical decisions, and he empowers us to use our resources effectively. Because of this, Jehovah assures us that we will never lack what we need.
13. Then, how can we observe carefully the birds of heaven?
13 Jesus asked a pointed question: "Are not five sparrows sold for two coins of very little value?" He then explained that not even one of them is forgotten by God. (Compare Luke 12:6, 7.) This illustration highlights Christ's concern for humble creatures. Jesus cares about the birds of heaven, and he certainly cares about us, because we are far more valuable to him.—Matt. 20:28.
14. What can help a person to avoid becoming overly concerned about material things?
14 Read Matthew 6:27. Jesus asked whether a person could lengthen his life span even a little by worrying. The reason why we should not worry is that our anxieties do not accomplish anything beneficial and only cause us distress. Therefore, avoiding unnecessary worry can contribute to our peace of mind.
15, 16. (a) How does knowing what Jehovah values help us to make wise decisions regarding material possessions? (See paragraph 7.) (b) What benefits do we experience when we are content, and why?
15 Read Matthew 6:28-30. Do you ever find yourself preoccupied with material things, wondering if you will have enough food or clothing? If so, remember that trusting in Jehovah is like saying, 'I am satisfied with just what I need.' Jesus encouraged us to focus on what Jehovah provides, rather than being anxious about material concerns. By appreciating "the lilies of the field," we learn to be content with what we have. Note how Jesus used the example of beautiful flowers (such as gladioli, hyacinths, irises, and tulips) that serve no practical purpose. These flowers simply beautify the earth. Are not humans much more valuable than such flowers? "And Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these!"
16 Let us now consider why Jesus asked: "Which of you, when he wants to give his child something good, would give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, does he give him a snake instead?" Clearly, a loving father would never do that! This illustrates how eager our heavenly Father is to give us good things. (Matt. 8:26; 14:31; 16:8; 17:20) So, let us continue to strengthen our faith and trust in Jehovah completely. What can help us to do so? By recognizing that Jehovah cares for us and is willing to support us during difficult times.
17. What can help us to maintain a close relationship with Jehovah?
17 Read Matthew 6:31, 32. We want to be among those who put "his kingdom first," because they know that Jehovah lovingly provides everything we need. To prioritize 'seeking first the kingdom' means strengthening our relationship with Jehovah. It shows that we value what is important to him. Jehovah will then bless our efforts. "The love of money" can distract us from this goal.—1 Tim. 6:6-8.
ARE WE SATISFIED WITH WHAT JEHOVAH PROVIDES?
18. How does Jehovah show that he cares for each of us individually, and what comfort does this bring us?
18 Read Matthew 6:33. Jesus taught his followers to focus on spiritual things, not material possessions. We should strive to imitate his attitude: "All these things others are seeking." What did he mean by "all these things"? See paragraph 32. He explained: 'Your Father knows that you need all these things.' These are the things people normally seek. Jehovah knows our needs—our necessities of life, such as food, clothing, and shelter—and he helps us satisfy them. (Prov. 4:19) Despite this, we may still worry. But we can trust that Jehovah will support us. We can also be sure that he will give us strength to cope with whatever challenges we face, even if we have very little materially.—Matt. 6:31-33.
19. So, how can we learn to appreciate what Jehovah provides?
19 Read Matthew 6:34. In his sermon, Jesus urged his listeners: "Quit being anxious." Let us examine why anxiety is harmful and how we can cultivate confidence in Jehovah's ability to care for us. A person who constantly worries about tomorrow is likely missing out on joy today and failing to show gratitude to God.—Phil. 3:5, 6; Prov. 4:6, 7.
TO FIND SATISFACTION IN LIFE AND PLEASE JEHOVAH
20. (a) What reason do we have for wanting to live in harmony with Jehovah's will? (b) How can we show that we value spiritual things?
20 As mentioned earlier, contentment comes from valuing what we have. Every time we give thanks, we demonstrate our appreciation for Jehovah's provisions. For example, when faced with a difficult decision, do you first seek counsel from experienced elders? Do you pray earnestly for guidance and then take steps to attend the School for Kingdom Evangelizers? Or do you carefully consider the requirements and apply to serve at Bethel or in a circuit assembly? Do you willingly cooperate with the local Construction Department? Regularly ask yourself, 'What practical steps can I take to support the work of proclaiming the good news?' And be determined to use each opportunity to share in this important activity. The brochure "How to Cope With Anxiety" may also prove helpful in your ministry. Review the suggestions and determine which ones you can put into practice.
21. What can you do to strengthen your relationship with Jehovah?
21 Jesus taught us to prioritize spiritual things over material possessions. We show our gratitude to Jehovah by being willing to sacrifice our comfort and convenience, even if it means giving up some of the things we enjoy, or facing difficulties. By focusing on storing up treasures with God, we demonstrate that we value his friendship and appreciate the hope he gives us. Also, regularly examine how we use our resources and strive to 'lay up for ourselves a fine foundation' for the future.—1 Tim. 6:19.
^ [1] (paragraph 12) To learn more about how Jehovah feels about Christians maintaining Christian neutrality, see the article "Why Remain Neutral?" in The Watchtower of October 1, 2014, pages 31–32.

text:
ĨLA naĩ na myaka 12 nĩw'o namanyie kana naĩ na kĩndũ kya vata mũno ndonya kũnenga angĩ. Ĩvinda yĩmwe twĩ ũmbanonĩ mũnene mwana-a-asa ũmwe nĩwangũlilye kana no nende kũtavany'a. O na kau ndyaĩ naatavany'a ĩvinda o na yĩmwe namũsũngĩie namwĩa: "Ĩĩ." Nĩtwaendie nĩ nake kĩsionĩ na anenga tũvuku tũmwe tũeleetye ĩũlũ wa Ũsumbĩ wa Ngai. Na ĩndĩ ambĩa: "Thi ũneenete na andũ ala me ngalĩko ĩĩya ya lelũ nakwa ndineena na ala me ngalĩko ĩno." O na kau naĩ na wia nĩnaendie nĩtavanĩtye nyũmba na nyũmba. Naseng'ie mũno nũndũ nanenganie tũvuku tũu tw'onthe o kwa ĩvinda ĩkuvĩ. Kwa w'o, andũ aingĩ nĩmendeeaw'a nĩ kĩla naĩ nakyo.
Nasyaĩwe taoni ya Chatham, ĩla yĩ kaondinĩ ya Kent, nthĩ ya England, mwaka wa 1923. Ĩvinda yĩu andũ aingĩ maĩ atũlĩku ngoo. Ũla Kaũ Mũnene ndwaaĩanĩsya wĩkwatyo ũla maĩ naw'o wa kana nthĩ nĩkũseũvanga. Namo asyai makwa nĩmatũlĩtwe ngoo nĩ atongoi ma ĩkanisa ya Baptist nũndũ kĩla atongoi asu mathĩnĩkĩaa mũno nĩ kwĩyambatya kĩlasi. Nĩ wa myaka kenda ũu, inyia-akwa nĩwambĩĩe kũthi nyũmbanĩ ya International Bible Students Association vala andũ amwe maĩ manambĩĩa kwĩtwa Ngũsĩ sya Yeova meekĩaa "ilasi," kana maũmbano moo. Ithyĩ ala twaĩ syana nĩtwambĩĩe kũmanyĩw'a Mbivilia nĩ mwĩĩtu-a-asa ũmwe atũmĩĩte ĩvuku The Harp of God vamwe na Mbivilia. Nĩnendeeiw'e mũno nĩ kĩla neemanyĩasya.
NGELEKANY'O YA ANA-A-ASA ALA AIMA NĨYANDETHISYE
Nĩ wa mũika nĩnatanĩaa mũno kũtavya andũ ĩũlũ wa wĩkwatyo ũla wĩ Ndetonĩ ya Ngai. O na kau mavinda maingĩ nĩnaendaa kũtavany'a nyũmba na nyũmba nĩ nyioka, ĩla natavany'a na andũ angĩ nĩneemanyĩasya maũndũ maingĩ. Kwa ngelekany'o, mũthenya ũmwe twatwaĩte isululu sitũ nĩ na mwana-a-asa ũmwe mũima tũendete kũtavany'a kĩsionĩ kĩmwe, na ĩla twavĩtũkie mũtongoi ũmwe wa ndĩni nasya: "Mbũi nĩsu!" Mwana-a-asa ũsu naĩ nake aũngamisye kĩsululu kyake na ambĩa twĩkale nthĩ kĩting'ĩnĩ kyaĩ vandũ. Twekala nthĩ angũlilye atĩĩ: "Nũũ ũla ũkũnengie ũkũmũ wa kũsilĩla andũ ũimetaa mbũi? Kĩla twaĩle kwĩka yu nĩ kũtanĩa kũtavya andũ ũvoo mũseo na tũieka Yeova amasilĩle nowe." Ĩvindanĩ yĩu naĩ wa mũika nĩneemanyĩisye maũndũ maingĩ mũno ĩũlũ wa ũtanu ũla mũndũ ũkwataa anengane.—Mt. 25:31-33; Meko 20:35.
Nake mwana-a-asa ũngĩ o mũima nĩwamanyĩisye kana nĩ kenda mũndũ akwate ũtanu ũla ũetawe nĩ kũnengane, mavinda amwe no nginya ethĩwe na wũmĩĩsyo. Ĩvinda yĩu kĩveti kyake kĩyendete Ngũsĩ sya Yeova. Mũthenya ũmwe mwana-a-asa ũsu nĩwanthokisye mũsyĩ kwake tũĩsanĩe. Nũndũ mwana-a-asa ũsu atindĩte ũtavany'a, kĩveti kyake kyathatie mũno na kyambĩĩa kũtũkimanga na vakiti sya maianĩ. Ĩndĩ vandũ va mwana-a-asa amũtetye, oosanisye vakiti isu na aitũnga nesa vala syaĩ e mũtanu. Ĩtina wa myaka, wũmĩĩsyo wake nĩwamũeteie ũathimo ĩla kĩveti kyake kyavatisiwe na kyatw'ĩka Ngũsĩ.
Wendi wakwa wa kũnenga angĩ wĩkwatyo wa ĩvinda yũkĩte nĩwaendeeie kwingĩva, na mũthya nĩ na inyia-akwa nĩtwavatisĩwe Dover, Mweinĩ wa 3, 1940. Ĩndĩ twĩ Mweinĩ wa 9, 1939, Britain nĩyatwie kũkita na Germany. Ĩvinda yĩu naĩ na myaka 16. Ĩtina wa kavinda, twĩ Mwei wa 6, 1940, nasyaisye nĩũngye mũomonĩ witũ noona asikalĩ ngili mbingĩ mũno mavĩtĩte na maloli. Asikalĩ asu moonekaa me atelemu mũno. Asu maĩ asikalĩ ala mavonokete kaũ weetawa Battle of Dunkirk. Mailyĩ ta andũ mate na wĩkwatyo, na kĩu nĩkyatumie nĩw'a nenda kũmatavya ĩũlũ wa Ũsumbĩ wa Ngai. Mwaka ũsu wangĩe kũthela, Germany nĩyambĩĩe kũkima Britain na mbomu. Kĩla ũtukũ nĩnoonaa ndeke sya Germany iũlũkĩle vakuvĩ na kwitũ iendete kũlekya mbomu kũndũ. Waĩ ũtonya kwĩw'a mbomu isu itheete, na nũndũ wa wasya mũnene ũla wew'ĩkaa syatũĩka, wia witũ nĩwongelekile. Mũthenya ũla ũatĩĩe twathi nza tweethĩaa nyũmba mbingĩ syanangiwe nĩ mbomu isu. Maũndũ asu matumie nĩmanya nesa kana ndyaĩ na wĩkwatyo ũngĩ eka Ũsumbĩ.
KWAMBĨĨA ŨTHŨKŨMI WA KŨNENGANE
Mwakanĩ wa 1941 nĩw'o nambĩĩe kũtethya wĩa ũla ũtumĩte nĩthĩwa nĩ mũtanu mũno. Ĩvindanĩ yĩu nathũkũmanaa na Royal Dockyard nĩ vandũ vetawa Chatham. Namanyĩaw'a ũndũ ndonya kũseũvya meli, na ũsu nĩ wĩa andũ maũmelealya mata mũno nũndũ waĩvĩte nesa. Kwa ĩvinda ĩasa athũkũmi ma Yeova nĩmeesĩ kana Aklĩsto mayaĩle kũkitĩa nthĩ o na yĩva. Ĩndĩ mwakanĩ wa 1941 ũu, nĩtwambĩĩe kũelewa kana tũyaĩle kũthũkũma kambunĩnĩ ĩkũseũvya mĩio ya kaũ. (Yoa. 18:36) Kwoou nũndũ nathũkũmaa kambunĩnĩ ya kũseũvya meli sya kaũ ila syĩsĩlaa ungu wa kĩw'ũ, nĩnatwie kũtia wĩa ũsu nĩ kana nĩlike ũthũkũminĩ wa ĩvinda yonthe. Mbee vyũ naendie kũtavany'a taoninĩ mbanake mũno yĩtawa Cirencester, ngalĩko ya Cotswolds.
Ĩla navikisye myaka 18 nĩnekiw'e yela nũndũ wa kũlea kũlika ũthũkũminĩ wa ita sya kaũ, na navekala myei kenda. Nakwatiwe nĩ wia mwingĩ mũno ĩla mũomo wa seli wavingiwe na natiwa vu nthĩnĩ nĩ nyioka. Ĩndĩ ĩtina wa ĩvinda ĩkuvĩ asikalĩ ma kũu na avungwa nĩmambĩĩe kũngũlya noovewe kĩ. Natanie mũno nũndũ wa kũkwata mwanya ũsu wa kũmaelesya mũĩkĩĩo wakwa.
Nathaw'a nĩnakũlilw'e ngatavany'e nĩ na Leonard Smith * taoninĩ syĩ kĩvathũkany'o sya kaondi yitũ ya Kent. Kuma mwaka wa 1944, ndeke mbee wa ngili ũmwe, ila syeethĩawa ite na mũndũ ũitwaĩte, nĩsyavalũkilw'e kaondinĩ ĩsu ya Kent. Ndeke isu syeethĩawa syusũĩtw'e mbomu nthĩnĩ. Isu syaĩ ndeke sya kyama kya Nazi na syesĩlaa kaondinĩ yitũ ya Kent iendete kũkima London. Mbomu ila syaĩ ndekenĩ isu syeetawa doodlebugs. Twekalaa tũtelemete nũndũ ĩla tweew'a ingyini ya ndeke yavoa, twamanyaa ĩtina wa sekendi nini nĩkũvalũkw'a na ĩilivũka. Ĩvinda yĩu ve mũsyĩ ũmwe wa andũ atano tweemanyĩasya Mbivilia namo. Mavinda amwe twasomeaa ungu wa mesa ya kyũma maseũvĩtye mevithae vo nĩ kana nyũmba yesa kũtumbũka maikaũmĩe. Onthe me atano nĩmesie kũvatiswa.
KŨTHAMĨĨA NTHĨ INGĨ KWONDŨ WA ŨVOO MŨSEO
Kaũ ũsu wathela nĩnakũnie ũvainia kwa ĩvinda ya myaka ĩlĩ nĩ ngalĩko ya ĩtheo ya kĩthama kĩtawa Ireland. Tũyeesĩ kaĩ kũtavany'a Ireland kwaĩ kĩvathũkany'o kĩnene na kũtavany'a England! Kwa ngelekany'o, nĩ kana tũkwate ũkomo, twaendie nyũmba na nyũmba tũitavya andũ kana ithyĩ twĩ amisonalĩ. O na lelũnĩ twaendaa tũnengete andũ makaseti maitũ. Nũndũ andũ aingĩ nthĩ ĩsu maĩ ma Katholeki, kwĩka ũu ko kũtaĩ ũndũ wa ũtũndũu mũno! Nĩngũlilikana ĩvinda mũndũũme ũmwe watũtĩsisye, na kwoou nathi kũtavya mũsikalĩ. Mũsikalĩ ũsu angũlilye, "Kwani inyw'ĩ mũithi vau tyo mwĩĩsĩ ũndũ veũthi?" O na tũyeesĩ kaĩ avea ma kũu me ũkũmũ mũnene! Nĩmatumaa andũ mavutwa wĩanĩ woo ethĩwa nĩmeetĩkĩla mavuku maitũ. O na nĩmatumie tũlũngw'a kũla twakomboete.
Ĩtina wa ĩvinda yĩte ĩasa nĩtwamanyie kana ĩla twakomboa nyũmba kĩsionĩ kĩna, ũndũ ũla waaĩle nĩ kũendaa kũtavany'a kĩsio kĩ vaasa na vau tũkomboete na kĩũngamĩwe nĩ mũvea wĩ kĩvathũkany'o. Ala me kĩsionĩ kĩla tũkomboete nyũmba nĩmo twesaa kũtavya ma mũthya. Kĩsionĩ kya Kilkenny vaĩ mwanake ũmwe tweemanyĩasya nake katatũ kwa kyumwa o na kau andũ nĩmaumĩlasya nduuthĩ. Natanĩie mũno kũmanyĩsya angĩ ũw'o ũla wĩ Mbivilianĩ nginya naamũa kũkũlya nĩthi Sukulu ya Mbivilia ya Ngileati.
Sukulu ĩsu yeekĩiwe New York kwa ĩvinda ya myei itano, na twamina nĩtwatũmiwe twĩ ana ithamanĩ nini ila syĩ Ũkanganĩ wa Caribbean. Nĩtwaumie New York City Mwei wa 11, mwakanĩ wa 1948, na twathi kũu na ĩsiwa ĩnene yeetawa Sibia yĩla yaĩ ya vuti 59 (mita 18). Ndyaĩ naathi na ĩsiwa, kwoou neew'aa nĩ na kĩvya kingĩ. Ũmwe witũ eetawa Gust Maki na aĩ mũtwai wa meli wĩ ũmanyi mwingĩ. Nĩwatũmanyĩisye maũndũ amwe makonetye kũtwaa ĩsiwa, ta ũndũ mũndũ ũtonya kwambatya na kũtheesya itambaa ila itetheeasya ĩsiwa kũthi, ũndũ mũndũ ũtonya kũmanya ngalĩ ĩla ũendete, na ũndũ ũtonya kũtwaa ĩsiwa ĩla kwĩ kĩseve. O na kau kwaĩ na iseve nthũku, Gust atwaie ĩsiwa yitũ nesa kwa mĩthenya 30 nginya twavika Bahamas.
'MĨTAVANY'EI ITHAMANĨ'
Ĩtina wa kũtavany'a ithamanĩ nini sya Bahamas kwa myei mĩvũthũ, nĩtwaendie na ĩsiwa kũtavany'a Ithamanĩ sya Leeward na sya Windward. Ithama isu syambĩĩe vakuvĩ na Ithama sya Virgin ila syĩ vakuvĩ na Puerto Rico, na ikathi ta maili 500 (kĩlomita 800) nginya ikew'a kũvika Trinidad. Twatavanisye ithamanĩ syĩ kĩvathũkany'o kwa ĩvinda ya myaka ĩtano. Ithamanĩ isu kũyaĩ Ngũsĩ. Mavinda amwe vavĩtaa syumwa siana ũna o na tũtesa kũtũma kana kũkwata valũa. Ĩndĩ nĩtwatanie mũno kũtavany'a ndeto ya Yeova ithamanĩ isu.—Yel. 31:10.
Twakilasya twaũngamya ĩsiwa yitũ ũtee wa ũkanga, ekali ma kũu makatũmbĩĩa mayenda kũtũmanya. Amwe moo mayaĩ maaona ĩsiwa ta yĩu, o na mayaĩ maaona mũsũngũ. Ekali ma ithama isu maĩ andũ aseo na mendete maũndũ ma ndĩni, o na nĩmeesĩ Mbivilia nesa. Mavinda maingĩ nĩmatũnengae makũyũ, mavakato, na nzũũ kalanga. O na kau ĩsiwa yitũ yaĩ o na mwanya mũnini wa kũkoma, kũua, na kũvũĩa ngũa, nĩtwaendeeie nesa.
Nĩtwaendaa mũthenya w'onthe kũthokea andũ ma ithama isu. Mũno mũno twamatavasya kana nĩkũĩthĩwa na ũvoo wa Mbivilia. Na ĩndĩ kwangĩe kũtuka nĩtwakũnaa ngengele ĩla yaĩ ĩsiwanĩ yitũ. Twatanaa mũno kwona ekali ma kũu mokĩte kwĩthukĩĩsya ũvoo ũsu. Waĩ ũtonya kwona taa syoo ikenete ta ndata matheeete kĩĩmanĩ. O na mavinda amwe nĩvookaa andũ ĩana na mayĩkala nginya ũtukũ maikũlya makũlyo. O na eka ũu, nĩmatanĩaa kwina mbathi sitũ na kwoou twamaandĩkĩaa ndeto sya mbathi imwe sya Ũsumbĩ na tũimanenge. Ithyĩ twĩ ana nĩtwatataa mũno kwina mbathi isu nesa na ĩndĩ andũ mamanya ũndũ sinawa mayoseleela. Mawasya moo moosanaa nesa vyũ na mawasya maitũ. Asu maĩ mavinda maseo ta kĩ!
Ĩtina wa kwĩmanyĩsya na amanyĩw'a amwe, nĩmatũatĩĩaa mũsyĩ ũla ũngĩ tũendete nĩ kana maendeee kwĩmanyĩsya. O na kau twaumaa kĩsionĩ kĩmwe ĩtina wa syumwa nini, mavinda maingĩ nĩtwakũlasya andũ ala mendeew'a mũno maendeee kwĩmanyĩsya na ala angĩ nginya ĩla twĩsyoka. Waĩ ũndũ wa kwendeesya mũno kwona ũndũ amwe moosaa kwa ũito kĩanda kĩu twamanengae.
Ũmũnthĩ mbingĩ sya ithama isu syĩthĩawa na syĩndũ mbingĩ sya kũtanĩthya atalii ĩndĩ ĩvindanĩ yĩu kũyaĩ andũ aingĩ, na kĩla waĩ ũtonya kũthi kwĩloela no maia manake me kĩw'ũ kĩkelemu, vamwe na nthangathĩ ila syĩ ndee wa ũkanga na mĩnathi. Mũno mũno twaendaa na ũtukũ kuma kĩthamanĩ kĩmwe kũthi kĩla kĩngĩ. Twoonaa dolphins iithaũkĩa vakuvĩ na ĩsiwa yitũ na wasya ũla waĩ ũtonya kwĩw'a no wa ĩsiwa yitũ yavũĩte kĩw'ũ. Naw'o mwei weethĩawa ũathĩte kĩw'ũ kya ũkanga ũkethĩa wĩona vailyĩ ta ve lelũ mũseo mũnene ũendete ũkathelekelya.
Ĩtina wa kũtavany'a ithamanĩ isu kwa myaka ĩtano, nĩtwaendie Puerto Rico kũtũnga ĩsiwa yĩla twaĩ nayo na tũyosa yĩ na ingyini. Twavika kũu nĩnakomanie na mwĩĩtu-a-asa mwanake weetawa Maxine Boyd ũla waĩ misonalĩ, na neew'a nendeew'a nĩwe. Maxine aĩ mũtavany'a wa ũvoo mũseo wĩ kĩthito kuma e kana kanini. Ĩla weanie nĩwatavanisye Dominican Republic e misonalĩ nginya mwakanĩ wa 1950, ĩla wesie kũlũngw'a kuma nthĩ ĩsu nĩ silikalĩ ya kũu, ĩla yatongoew'e nĩ ĩkanisa ya Katholeki. Neetĩkĩlĩtw'e kwĩkala Puerto Rico kwa ĩvinda ya mwei ũmwe nũndũ nalikĩte kw'o ta mũthũkũmi wa melinĩ. Ĩtina wa mwei ũsu naaĩlĩte kũsyoka naku ithamanĩ na ndyĩkala kw'o kwa myaka ĩana ũna. Na kwoou nĩnambĩĩe kũsũanĩa ũũ: 'Ronald, ethĩwa nũkwenda mwĩĩtu ũũ, nĩwaĩle kũtumũa nake mĩtũkĩ.' Ĩtina wa syumwa itatũ nĩnakũlilye Maxine ethĩwa no tũtwaane, na ĩndĩ syumwa thanthatũ iithela twatwaana. Twatũmiwe Puerto Rico ta amisonalĩ nĩ nake na kwoou ndyaasama yĩla ĩsiwa twalatĩtye.
Mwakanĩ wa 1956 nĩtwambĩĩe kũthokea ikundi nĩ mũsyaĩĩsya wa mũthyũlũlũko. Ikundinĩ ila twaendaa ana-a-asa aingĩ maĩ ngya ĩndĩ nĩtwendete kũmathokea. Kwa ngelekany'o, ndũanĩ ĩmwe yĩtawa Potala Pastillo, vaĩ mĩsyĩ ĩlĩ ya Ngũsĩ sya Yeova yaĩ na syana mbingĩ na nĩnendete kũivuvĩa mũtũlilũ. Ĩvinda yĩmwe nĩnakũlilye kelĩtu kamwe keetawa Hilda kana no kende kũka tũkatavany'e nako. Kambĩie: "No nende ĩndĩ vaitonyeka nũndũ ndi na iatũ." Nĩtwakathooeie iatũ na twathi ũtavany'a nako. Ĩtina wa ĩvinda, mwakanĩ wa 1972, nĩ na Maxine nĩtwatembeie Mbetheli ya Brooklyn na twĩ kũu nĩtwoonie mwĩĩtu-a-asa ũmwe waĩ anamina Sukulu ya Ngileati okĩte kũtũtumũsya. Eeteele kũthi kũtavany'a Ecuador kũla waĩ anatũmwa. Atũkũlilye: "Ti ta mũũkwatya ninyie ũũ, ti w'o? Ninyie kala kelĩtu ka Pastillo kataĩ na iatũ." Kaĩ aĩ Hilda! Twatanie mũno nginya twaĩa!
Mwaka wa 1960 nĩtwakũlilw'e tũkathũkũme ovisinĩ wa ũvonge wa Puerto Rico, ũla waĩ nyũmbanĩ nini ya ngolova ilĩ ngalĩko ya Santurce, taoninĩ ya San Juan. Mbeenĩ nĩ na mwana-a-asa Lennart Johnson nithyĩ twatethasya wĩa ũla mwingĩ. Lennart na mũka nĩmo maĩ Ngũsĩ sya mbee nthĩ ya Dominican Republic, na mookie nthĩ ya Puerto Rico mwakanĩ wa 1957. Ĩtina Maxine nĩwambĩĩe kũtũma makaseti kwa andũ ala maandĩkĩthĩtye matũmĩawe, na atũmaa makaseti mbee wa ngili ũmwe kĩla kyumwa. Nĩwatanĩaa mũno kũthũkũma wĩa ũsu nũndũ asũanĩaa ĩũlũ wa andũ asu onthe meũkwata lĩu wa kĩ-veva.
Nĩnĩtanĩaa kũthũkũma Mbetheli nũndũ nĩthĩawa ngĩnenga andũ angĩ kĩla nĩ nakyo. Ĩndĩ no ngomanaa na mawetu. Kwa ngelekany'o, ĩvinda ya ũmbano mũnene wa nthĩ mbingĩ ũla weekĩiwe Puerto Rico mwakanĩ wa 1967 kwa ĩvinda ya mbee, neew'aa nĩ mũemeee mũno nĩ kĩanda kĩla naĩ nakyo. Nathan Knorr, ũla waũngamĩe wĩa wa Ngũsĩ sya Yeova ĩvindanĩ yĩu, nĩwookie Puerto Rico. Asũanĩie kana ndyavangĩthĩtye ũndũ amisonalĩ ala mathokete nthĩ ĩsu mekũvika vala tweekĩaa ũmbano na ũndũ mesaa kwĩnũka o na kau nĩneekĩte ũu. Ĩtina nĩwanengie ũtao mũito ĩũlũ wa kũvangĩthya maũndũ nesa na atia ambĩa atĩ nĩnamũtũla ngoo. Ndyaaenda kũkananĩa nake ĩndĩ neewie ambosa naĩ na nĩnekalangile o kwa ĩvinda ndyĩw'a woo. Ĩndĩ o na ũu wĩ o vo, ĩla Maxine nakwa twesie kũkomana ĩngĩ na Mwana-a-asa Knorr, nĩwatũthokisye kwake na atũuĩa lĩu.
Twĩ Puerto Rico nĩtwaendangaa England kũkethya andũ ma mũsyĩ. Tata ndaaĩtĩkĩla ũw'o ĩvinda yĩla nĩ na inyia-akwa twawĩtĩkĩlile. Ĩndĩ ĩla ana-a-asa kuma Mbetheli mooka kumya ũvoo, Mami nĩwamathokasya makomele kwitũ. Tata nĩwoonaa ũndũ ana-a-asa asu kuma Mbetheli meethĩawa na wĩnyivyo maelekanw'a na atongoi ma ndĩni ingĩ ala mamũthatĩtye myaka yĩ navu ĩtina. Kwoou mwakanĩ wa 1962 nĩwavatisiwe atw'ĩka Ngũsĩ.
Kĩveti kyakwa, Maxine, kyakwie mwakanĩ wa 2011. Neteele mũno kũmwona ĩngĩ ĩvindanĩ ya ũthayũũkyo. Ko ndew'aa mũyo mũno nasũanĩa ũndũ ũsu! Kwa ĩvinda ya myaka 58 yĩla nekalile na Maxine, nĩtwoonie ũndũ andũ ma Yeova mongelekile nthĩ ya Puerto Rico. Mongelekile kuma 650 ũu nginya 26,000! Mwakanĩ wa 2013 ovisi wa ũvonge wa Puerto Rico nĩwatũngĩanĩiwe na ũla wa Amelika na nakũlw'a ngathũkũme Wallkill, New York. Nekalile myaka 60 kĩthamanĩ kya Puerto Rico nginya weethĩa nĩĩw'a navikie mũsyĩ ta kala kola ka kũu ketawa coquí. Kola kau kambaa ko-kee, ko-kee ĩla kwatuka. Kesĩkĩe mũno kũu na kendete kwĩkala mĩtĩnĩ. Ĩndĩ yu ĩvinda yaĩ yĩnavika ya kuma kũu.
"NGAI ENDETE MŨNDŨ ŨNENGANAE NA ŨTANU"
O na yu no nĩtanĩaa kũthũkũma Ngai nĩ Mbetheli. Nĩ na myaka mbee wa 90, na nĩnengetwe wĩa wa kwĩkĩa ana-a-asa ala mathũkũmaa Mbetheli vinya. Nĩawa kana kuma ĩla nookie Wallkill nĩkĩĩte ana-a-asa mbee wa 600 vinya. Amwe mokaa kũmbona tũneenee mathĩna moo ene kana o mathĩna ma mũsyĩ. Angĩ mangũlasya nĩmanenge ũtao wa ũndũ matonya kũthũkũma nesa wĩa ũla manengetwe Mbetheli. O namo ala matwaana mĩtũkĩ nĩmangũlasya nĩmanenge ũtao ĩũlũ wa mũtwaano. Na ĩndĩ angĩ mangũlasya ũtao nĩ ala manaumiw'e Mbetheli na matũmwa ta mavainia. Nĩnĩthukĩĩasya andũ onthe ala mooka kũneena nakwa, na mavinda maingĩ noona vaĩle nĩmeaa: "'Ngai endete mũndũ ũnenganae na ũtanu.' Kwoou tanĩa wĩa waku, nũndũ wĩthĩawa ũimũthũkũma Yeova."—2 Ako. 9:7.
Nĩ kana ũtanĩe kũthũkũma Mbetheli, no nginya wĩkale ũisũanĩa nĩkĩ wĩa ũla ũũtethya nĩ wa vata. Ũndũ ũsu now'o wendekaa ĩla wĩ ũthũkũminĩ wa mĩthemba ĩngĩ. Wĩa w'onthe ũla tũtethasya Mbetheli nĩ wĩa wa Ngai. Na ĩla tũũtethya wĩa ũsu twĩthĩawa tũitetheesya "ngombo yĩ na kĩthito na mbũĩ" kũnenga ana-a-asa lĩu wa kĩ-veva nthĩ yonthe. (Mt. 24:45) Ĩndĩ kĩla vandũ o na va tũũmũthũkũmĩa Yeova nĩtwĩthĩawa na myanya mĩseo ya kũmũkumya. Kwoou ekai ithyonthe tũtanĩe wĩa w'onthe ũla ũtũnengete nũndũ "Ngai endete mũndũ ũnenganae na ũtanu."
^ kal. 13 Ngewa ya Leonard Smith ĩeleetw'e ĩkasetinĩ ya Mũsyaĩĩsya (Kĩswaili) ya 15/04/2012.

translation:
When I was 12 years old, I realized that I had something special that could help people. One day, we were visiting a large hospital and I saw a child who seemed very sad and I felt sorry for him. And then I thought I couldn't help him, and another time I told him this: "It is okay." I went with my mother and we found a small church where we prayed to God. And she told me: "Go and comfort others like yourself because I have comforted you." And then when I grew up I started going from house to house. I helped many people and I found joy in doing so for the first time. Because of that, many people appreciated what I did.
I was born in Chatham, Kent, England in 1923. That place was known to many people. My grandfather was a carpenter, but he also worked as a farmer sometimes. He taught me how to work and I enjoyed helping him with his farming tasks. At around ten years old, my parents told me about the International Bible Students Association, which some people called "the class" or "the society." We all learned to study the Bible using a book called The Harp of God along with the Bible. I liked it and I continued learning.
NOTICE TO CHILDREN WHO ARE INTERESTED
It was during that time that I began to visit people telling them about God's Kingdom. And although I visited many houses alone, I often went with others and we learned many things. For example, one day we were walking down a street with a child when we came across a certain house and heard someone shout: "Dogs!" That child was frightened and asked us to go back because of those dogs. We went back and he said: "Why are you still trying to tell people about the truth when they hate dogs so much? If we go near them, they will chase us away and we won't be able to let Jehovah save them." That experience taught me many things about the attitude of people who oppose the good news.—Matt. 25:31-33; Mark 20:35.
Later, another child told me that he was afraid of people who opposed the truth and some of his friends had mocked him. That experience led him to think seriously about serving Jehovah. One day that child became very sad and started to cry, and he said that he did not want to associate with bad people anymore. The people of that child pitied him, comforted him and encouraged him to continue in the truth. Over the years, his faith grew stronger and his heart remained attached to Jehovah.
My father's desire to preach led him to travel extensively, and in May we were transferred to Dover, England, on March 3, 1940. By September 9, 1939, Britain was at war with Germany. I was then 16 years old. In June 1940, we witnessed something amazing—our neighbor and others were rescued from France by small boats and destroyers. Those soldiers looked very tired. They were among those evacuated during what came to be known as the Battle of Dunkirk. Many of those men and their rescue were used to encourage us to continue supporting God's Kingdom. That year proved difficult, as Germany began bombing Britain. Every night we could hear German planes flying overhead and dropping bombs nearby. We often prayed that the bombs would miss us, and thankfully our house was spared, although our neighborhood suffered damage. One evening we ran to the basement when bombs fell near our home. These experiences helped me appreciate more fully the importance of remaining neutral in World War II.
BEGINNING OF THE WAR
WORK
In 1941, I was called up to do work considered essential to the war effort. This involved working at the Royal Dockyard in a town called Chatham. I learned how to repair ships, and this meant working long hours under pressure. During that time, Jehovah's Witnesses were persecuted because they remained neutral. In 1941, we had to decide whether we would apply for conscientious objector status. (John 18:36) Although I worked repairing warships, I felt that this did not compromise my neutrality, and I continued to feel that way throughout the war. Later, I was transferred to a large estate near Cirencester, in the Cotswolds.
After completing my 18th birthday, I volunteered for full-time service, and I enjoyed that very much. I was assigned to a circuit that included many rural areas, and I traveled mostly by bicycle. Once, while walking along a country road, I was frightened by a snake. On one occasion, during a severe storm, some soldiers took shelter in a barn and asked me to give a talk. I gladly accepted the opportunity to share my beliefs with them.
I remember being interviewed by Leonard Smith, a member of the local branch office in Kent. In 1944, I was called up again, but instead of being sent to the armed forces, I was directed to work in another part of Kent. This new assignment involved operating searchlights. These searchlights were used to try to shoot down German planes flying over Kent on their way to bomb London. These planes were also known as doodlebugs. We would watch anxiously for the sound of an approaching plane, knowing that within seconds it could be hit and fall. That year five of us shared in witnessing to people about the Bible. Sometimes we read a portion of scripture to people who invited us into their homes. Of those five, only one was baptized.
TO SHOW FURTHER GRATITUDE FOR THE TRUTH
One time I traveled to visit a family who lived near a small town in northern Ireland. We tried to reach them in Ireland with a large publication and then to reach them in England! For example, we sometimes had to go from house to house asking people if they wanted literature or if they knew someone who did. And often we found people willing to listen to our message. Many of these people were Catholics, yet they appreciated our presentation of the truth! I recall one instance where a man questioned us, and he asked us why we were interested in spiritual things. And we were able to show him something important from the scriptures! It motivated people to investigate our teachings further. And it motivated us to continue to make progress.
During that trip we learned whether or not we could find houses easily, which was difficult because going to find a place was complicated and we needed help from a local publisher. But when we found houses, that's when we began to ask about needs. The people of Kilkenny once told one of our brothers a story about three young men who went out drinking and some people made fun of them. I also remember learning about another brother from Mbiviliani who used to eat at the Mbivilia School of Gilead.
That school was located in New York for five months, and we were sent there with eight others, but only until the Caribbean Congregation. I arrived in New York City on November 11, 1948, and we sailed on a large ship called Siberia, which was 59 feet (18 meters) wide. After leaving the island, I felt seasick again. One of us was named Gust Maki and he was an experienced sailor. He taught us some things about sailing, such as how a person should not be afraid to hold onto and loosen the sails to make the ship move forward, how a person should know where they are going, and how a person should not sail the ship into danger. And sometimes, even with danger, Gust would sail our ship safely for 30 minutes until we reached the Bahamas.
'FINDING HOUSES EASILY'
The work of finding houses easily in the Bahamas for several months, I went around the islands to find houses in the Leeward Islands and the Windward Islands. These islands are close to the Virgin Islands but not to Puerto Rico, and it is about 500 miles (800 kilometers) to reach Trinidad. We found houses easily for five years. These houses went north. Some places had no water and we had to send or get containers. But we continued to find good houses to preach.—Jer. 31:10.
We often enjoyed our island life, especially because it helped us to learn more about people. Sometimes people saw the island as beautiful, and sometimes they saw it as desolate. Because of these islands, people learned many important things, and I also read the Bible more. Many islands had hills, valleys, and sandy beaches. And even though our island had plenty of room to walk, eat, and rest, we still traveled.
I want to help those who live on these islands. This is why we try to be guided by the principles of the Bible. And I hope to continue to visit the islands we have visited. We should always remember how important it is to apply these principles. It is easy to see that some places are better than others. And some people lived in small houses and spent their nights talking. And so, I was happy to write letters to my brothers and sisters and to encourage them. Now we can continue to write letters to our brothers and sisters and to help those who need encouragement. The stories they tell are very interesting.
The work of associating with fellow worshipers helps us to strengthen ourselves and to continue strengthening ourselves. And even when we face difficulties, many people enjoy helping others to strengthen themselves and others like them. It is easy to forget what we have learned when we spend too much time doing something else.
Many islanders are influenced by many things that distract them from paying attention to God's Word and leading many people astray, and sometimes they do not listen to good advice because of pride and stubbornness. So we must go out at night and preach the good news to everyone. We saw dolphins jumping around our island and enjoyed the beauty of our island. Also, yesterday I saw a large whale swimming near our island. It was amazing to see such a huge creature moving gracefully through the water.
I have been traveling to islands for five years now, and we went to Puerto Rico to visit an island we had heard about and explore it with others. We stayed there and met a wonderful woman named Maxine Boyd who was very kind, and we became friends with her. Maxine has been traveling extensively throughout the world and has visited many places. She once traveled to the Dominican Republic in the 1950s, but she returned home because she missed her family and church, which was Catholic. We spent only a month in Puerto Rico, but I enjoyed being there and meeting the local people. After that month, I continued traveling for another two years. And then I told myself this: 'Ronald, if you want to help this person, you need to send them money.' After three days, I called Maxine and asked her to meet me, and on the sixth day, we met. We were invited to Puerto Rico again as guests, and that's when I realized how beautiful the island we had talked about really was.
In 1956, we decided to leave the group and become pioneers. This group included many wonderful people, and we enjoyed working with them. For example, there was a man named Potala Pastillo, who was one of Jehovah's Witnesses and had many children, and I enjoyed talking to him. One day, I met a woman named Hilda, and she encouraged us to continue traveling. She said: "Don't worry, you can stay here as long as you like." So we stayed and continued traveling. Then, in 1972, Maxine and I visited Bethel in Brooklyn and learned about a wonderful brother who had graduated from Gilead School and was being sent out. He was going to Ecuador as a missionary. He told us: "Don't be afraid of you, right? You lived with Pastillo and his family." Oh, Hilda! We had a good time together!
In 1960, we were assigned to serve in the circuit of Puerto Rico, which covered several congregations, including the Santurce congregation in San Juan. At that time, I was with my son Lennart Johnson, and we traveled extensively. Lennart and his wife were also pioneers in the Dominican Republic, and they moved to Puerto Rico in 1957. Later, Maxine began sending cassette tapes to those who could not read, and she sent out many cassettes, one each month. I appreciated her efforts to reach those who did not know how to read.
I also appreciated being able to visit Bethel whenever possible. I enjoyed talking to the brothers there. For example, during a large assembly held in Puerto Rico in 1967, because of the size of the crowd, we had to take turns attending sessions. However, I always made sure to attend each session. Nathan Knorr, who supervised the work of Jehovah's Witnesses worldwide, visited Puerto Rico. He asked whether we felt personally responsible for helping those who attended the assemblies and whether we felt that we should make arrangements so that they would not have to leave without food. Later, he expressed his appreciation for our willingness to help others. I remember feeling very happy when he said that. Also, both Maxine and I enjoyed associating with Brother Knorr, and we often visited him.
After Puerto Rico, we were assigned to England to preach to people of many nationalities. Father was very pleased that we were given this assignment. But soon after arriving in England, Mother became seriously ill. Father realized that she needed more medical attention than could be provided locally, so he took her back to Bethel temporarily. During 1962, I was invited to serve at Bethel.
Maxine passed away in 2011. I look forward to seeing her again in the resurrection. How I miss her dearly! After 58 years of marriage to Maxine, we saw how much Jehovah's people grew in Puerto Rico. They increased from about 650 to over 26,000! In 2013, the branch office in Puerto Rico was renovated with funds donated by Christians in America and then rededicated at Wallkill, New York. Having lived in Puerto Rico for 60 years, I still enjoy hearing the sound of the coquí frog. That little frog makes a "co-kee, co-kee" sound that is quite distinctive. It is a pleasant sound to fall asleep to. And now, even though I am older, I still enjoy visiting the mountains.
I often think about those happy times spent in the mountains.
"GOD IS ONE WHO MAKES THINGS POSSIBLE"
Even now, I try to remain busy serving Jehovah at Bethel. I am almost 90 years old, and I appreciate being able to associate with so many young ones who are full-time ministers. At times, when I visit Wallkill, I meet with some 600 of them. Some come up to me and share their experiences, which are often heartwarming. Others express their gratitude for the spiritual food they receive from Bethel. Still others tell me about their challenges and ask for advice. I have learned that many people are willing to listen, and I find great satisfaction in offering encouragement. Often they respond positively to Bible counsel.—2 Cor. 9:7.
If you love Bethel, may you always strive to be exemplary in all that you say and do. This will help you to continue enjoying God's favor. And as we speak well of our ministry, we show ourselves to be "loyal and discreet slaves" who feed his household at the proper time. (Matt. 24:45) As each one of us endeavors to please Jehovah, we will be strengthened in our determination to keep preaching. Let us all continue to proclaim: "God is one who makes things possible."
^ par. 13 Letter from Leonard Smith received via the Branch Office (Swahili) dated April 15, 2012.

text:
Ĩandĩko yitũ ya 2018: "Ala mamweteelaa Yeova makeeũvw'a vinya woo."—ISA. 40:31.
MBATHI: 152, 51
1. Nĩ maũndũ meva tũng'ang'anaa namo, ĩndĩ nĩ kyaũ kĩtumaa Yeova endeew'a nĩ athũkũmi make aĩkĩĩku? (Sisya visa ĩthangũnĩ yĩĩ.)
O TONDŨ twĩsĩ, nthĩ ĩno tũtwĩe yĩ mathĩna maingĩ. Aingĩ menyu, inyw'ĩ ana-a-asa na eĩtu-a-asa endwa, nĩmũthĩnaw'a mũno nĩ mowau. Angĩ namo nĩmasũvĩaa andũ akũũ ma mũsyĩ o na kũtw'ĩka mo ene ti mo me na myaka mĩnini. Na ve angĩ mang'ang'anaa mũno kũmanthĩa mĩsyĩ yoo, na ti atĩ methĩawa masembanĩtye na syĩndũ ite sya lasima, ĩndĩ no mavata ala mataema kwĩanĩw'a. Kũthũkya ũvoo nĩtwĩsĩ kana aingĩ maithĩnaw'a no ũndũ ũmwe katĩ wa asu twaweta, ĩndĩ makũnĩtwe nĩ onthe savalĩ ũmwe! Asu nĩ maũndũ maminaa mũndũ vinya vyũ na makosa ĩvinda yingĩ mũno. Na ũimanya o na tũinaweta ngalama ĩla ĩlikaa ya mbesa. Ĩndĩ o na ũu wĩ o vo, mũĩkĩĩo wenyu wa kana Ngai akeanĩsya mawatho make nĩ mũlũmu vyũ, na mũi na nzika nongi kana ĩvinda yũkĩte maũndũ makaseũva. Mwĩona Yeova ta ũtanaa mũno wĩana ata oona ũu?
2. Ĩandĩko ya Isaia 40:29 yĩtwĩkĩaa vinya ata, ĩndĩ tũkaema kwĩsũvĩa nĩ ũndũ wĩva ũte mũseo tũtonya kwĩka?
2 Ĩndĩ we nĩwĩsaa kũvika vandũ ũkew'a ũvinyĩĩwe mũno nĩ mathĩna nginya ũkethĩa o na ndũveva? Ethĩwa nĩwĩsaa kwĩw'a ũu, manya kana tuuwe wĩ weka. O na Mbivilia nĩyonanĩtye kana athũkũmi aĩkĩĩku ma Ngai ma tene no mesaa kwĩw'a ta mavika mwĩso. (1 Asu. 19:4; Yovu 7:7) Ĩndĩ vandũ va kwĩkya ngoo, nĩmeekwatasya Yeova amanenge vinya. Na mayaasonoka nũndũ Ngai "nũmanengae vinya ala meũnyala." (Isa. 40:29) Ũndũ wa kyeva nĩ kana amwe ma andũ ma Ngai ũmũnthĩ mavikĩte vandũ makavanga atĩ meamba 'kũtia ũw'o mose nzeve.' Masũanĩaa ĩsu ta yo nzĩa ĩla nzeo ya kũmina mathĩna, nũndũ nĩ ta monaa kũthũkũma Yeova ta mũio vandũ va kwona ta ũathimo. Nũndũ wa ũu, nĩmaekaa kũsoma Ndeto ya Ngai, kũthi maũmbanonĩ, na kũtavany'a. Kĩu nĩkyo Satani wendaa.
3. (a) Tũtonya kũsiĩĩa Satani ata ndakonzye mũĩkĩĩo witũ? (b) Twĩneenea kyaũ ĩsomonĩ yĩĩ?
3 Ndevili nĩwĩsĩ nesa vyũ kana tweethĩwa na maũndũ maingĩ ma kwĩka ũthũkũminĩ wa Yeova tũkeethĩawa twĩ alũmu, nake ndendaa kwona twĩ alũmu. Wesa kwĩw'a mwĩĩ waku ũiemeewa kana ngoo yaku ĩitavĩwe vyũ, mwa ndũkaatate kũmũtia Yeova. Endeea kũmũthengeea mavinda onthe nũndũ 'akaũlũlũmĩlya, na aikwĩkĩa vinya.' (1 Vet. 5:10; Yak. 4:8) Ĩsomonĩ yĩĩ nĩtũkwona maũndũ elĩ matonya kũtuma tũleela ũthũkũminĩ witũ, na ĩndĩ tũineenea ũndũ myolooto ya Mbivilia ĩtonya kũtũtetheesya kũmĩĩsya. Ĩndĩ ekai twambe kũneenea ĩandĩko ya Isaia 40:26-31, yĩla yonanĩtye kana Yeova e ũtonyi wa kũtũũmĩĩsya.
ALA MAMWETEELAA YEOVA MAKEEŨVW'A VINYA WOO
4. Nĩ ũndũ wĩva tũtonya kwĩmanyĩsya nthĩnĩ wa Isaia 40:26?
4 Soma Isaia 40:26. Vai mũndũ waaĩsa kwĩthĩwa atonya kũtala ndata syonthe ila syĩ kw'o. Andũ ma saenzi maĩkĩĩaa kana kĩkundi kya ndata na syĩndũ ingĩ ila syĩ vamwe na nthĩ yitũ (Milky Way galaxy), nĩkĩtonya kwĩthĩwa kĩ na ndata itonya kũvika mbilioni 400. Ĩndĩ Yeova nũnengete kĩla ndata ĩsyĩtwa. Kĩu kĩtũmanyĩsya kyaũ? Yeova nũsianasya na syĩndũ ite thayũ ila woombie. Ethĩwa nĩwĩkaa ũu, we wĩona ta ũkwonaa ata we ũmũthũkũmaa nũndũ nũmwendete na ti kwĩthĩwa ndwĩ na wĩkwa? (Sav. 19:1, 3, 14) Ĩthe witũ wĩ wendo nũkwĩsĩ nesa vyũ. Mbivilia yaĩtye atĩĩ: "O na nzw'ĩĩ syonthe sya mĩtwe yenyu nĩ ndale." (Mt. 10:30) Nake mũandĩki wa Savuli atũĩkĩĩthĩtye ũũ: "Yeova nĩwe wĩsĩ mĩthenya ya ala eanĩu," kana kwa ndeto ingĩ, nĩwĩsĩ mathĩna ala makomanaa namo. (Sav. 37:18) Vate nzika, nĩwonaa mathĩna ala maũkwataa, na nũtonya kũũnenga vinya nĩ kana ũmĩĩsye thĩna o na wĩva.
5. Nĩ ũndũ wĩva ũtũĩkĩĩthasya kana Yeova nũtonya kũtũnenga vinya?
5 Soma Isaia 40:28. Vinya w'onthe wumaa kwa Yeova. Kwasũanĩa vinya ũla ũnengae syũa yĩ yoka. Mũandĩki ũmwe wa maũndũ ma saenzi wĩtawa David Bodanis aĩtye: 'Kĩla sekendi syũa yumasya vinya wĩanene na mũlivũko wa mbomu mbilioni mbingĩ sya atomu.' Nake mũsomi ũngĩ wĩkaa ũkunĩkĩli wa syĩndũ eekie ĩsavu ya vinya ũla syũa yumasya eethĩa kana "ũmũnthĩ yumasya vinya . . . ũtoetye kwĩanĩsya mavata ma andũ kwa kĩlungu kya myaka 200,000 nthĩnĩ wa sekendi o ĩmwe"! Vo ve mũndũ waĩle kwĩthĩwa na nzika kana ũla ũnengae syũa vinya nũtonya kũtũnenga vinya ũtwĩanĩtye nĩ kana tũmĩĩsye thĩna o na wĩva?
6. Nĩkĩ tũtonya kwasya kana ĩsoki ya Yesũ yĩi vinya kũkua, na kũmanya ũu kwaĩle kũtũtethya ata?
6 Soma Isaia 40:29. Kũmũthũkũma Yeova kũtũeteae ũtanu mwingĩ mũno. Yesũ eeie amanyĩw'a make atĩĩ: "Ĩyĩkĩei ĩsoki yakwa." Na ongela kwasya: "Mũkasyonea ngoo syenyu ũthũmũo. Nũndũ ĩsoki yakwa yĩti vinya, na mũio wakwa naw'o nĩ mũvũthũ." (Mt. 11:28-30) Ndeto isu nĩ sya w'o vyũ! Mavinda amwe tũendete ũmbanonĩ kana ũtavany'a, tumaa mũsyĩ tũyĩw'a twĩ anou vyũ. Ĩndĩ tũsyokaa mũsyĩ twĩw'ĩte ata? Tũsyokaa tũyĩw'a twĩ athũmũsye na twĩ na vinya wa kũkitana na mathĩna. Vate nzika, ĩsoki ya Yesũ yĩi vinya kũkua!
7. Elesya ũndũ wonekete ũkwonany'a ũw'o wa ĩandĩko ya Mathayo 11:28-30.
7 Mwĩĩtu-a-asa ũmwe tũũmwĩta Kayla ethĩĩtwe na ũwau ũtumaa ekala e na mĩnoo mingĩ, ũwau wa kũkw'a ngoo (depression), na nĩwalaw'a nĩ mũtwe mũthũku mũno. Mavinda amwe nũemawa nĩ kũthi maũmbanonĩ ma kĩkundi, na nengĩ nĩtũkũelewa nĩkĩ. Ĩndĩ mũthenya ũmwe nĩwang'ang'anie athi ũmbano. Ĩtina wa ũmbano ũsu aandĩkie atĩĩ: "Ũvoo ũla wumiw'e wĩĩkonetye [thĩna wa] kũkw'a ngoo. Wumiw'e kwa nzĩa ĩtumie nĩw'a nĩngũeleeka ũndũ ngwĩw'a na nĩngũthĩnĩkĩwa nginya netĩkya methoi. Kĩu kĩndilikanisye kana nĩnaĩlĩte kwĩthĩawa maũmbanonĩ." Mwĩĩtu-a-asa ũsu atanie mũno nũndũ nĩweekĩie kĩthito athi ũmbanonĩ.
8, 9. Mũtũmwa Vaulo endaa kwasya ata ĩla waandĩkie: "Yĩla nĩ mwonzu, nĩvo nĩ na vinya"?
8 Soma Isaia 40:30. O na tũkethĩwa twĩsĩ maũndũ maingĩvĩte ata, kĩla tũtonya kwĩanĩsya tũtũmĩĩte vinya witũ nĩ kĩnini. Ũsu nĩw'o ũndũ ũla wa vata twaĩle kwĩkala twĩsĩ. O na vala ve maũndũ maingĩ mũtũmwa Vaulo waĩ atonya kwĩka, ve maũndũ angĩ ũtaĩ eanĩsya na vinya wake. Ĩla Vaulo waeleisye Ngai mathĩna make, eeiwe atĩĩ: "Vinya wakwa wĩanĩe vala ve wonzu." Vaulo nĩwaeleiwe nĩ kĩla watavaw'a. Ĩtina aisye atĩĩ: "Yĩla nĩ mwonzu, nĩvo nĩ na vinya." (2 Ako. 12:7-10) We Vaulo endaa kwasya ata?
9 Vaulo eethĩie kana ndaĩ eanĩsya maũndũ maingĩ atatetheew'e nĩ vinya ũngĩ mwingangĩ. Veva mũtheu wa Ngai waĩ ũtonya kũmũnenga vinya ĩla ũkwĩw'a e mwonzu. Na ti ũu wĩ w'oka, ĩndĩ veva ũsu waĩ ũtonya kũmũtetheesya eke maũndũ o na ũtaĩ esa kwĩka na vinya wake mwene. Tũi kĩvathũkany'o na Vaulo. Kwoou ethĩwa vinya ũla twĩ naw'o umĩte kwa Yeova, tũkekalaa twĩ alũmu!
10. Yeova amũtetheeisye Ndaviti ata omĩanĩsye na mawetu ala wakomanaa namo?
10 Mũandĩki wa Savuli, Ndaviti, nĩwoonaa ũndũ veva mũtheu wa Ngai wamũtethasya mũno. Ainie asya atĩĩ: "Kwondũ waku nĩngũvũthũa nguthu; na kwondũ wa Ngai wakwa nĩngũthaanyũka ũvai." (Sav. 18:29) Mathĩna amwe methĩawa me momũ mũno ta ũvai, kana ũkũta, ũkethĩa o na tũyĩsa 'kũmathaanyũka' na vinya witũ tũtatetheew'e nĩ Yeova.
11. Elesya ũndũ veva mũtheu ũtũtetheeasya kũmĩanĩsya na mathĩna maitũ.
11 Soma Isaia 40:31. Ndiũ yĩthĩawa ĩtonya kwambata na ĩkathi kũndũ kũasa mũno o ĩlelete kĩsevenĩ, ĩndĩ ndĩkaa ũu kwa vinya wayo wĩ w'oka. Ĩla nzeve mbyũ yambatĩte nĩtetheeasya ndiũ kwambata kũvika vala ĩkwenda na nũndũ wa ũu ĩiũlũka ĩtũmĩĩte vinya mũnini. Kwoou ĩla wesa kũkomana na maũndũ maito lilikanaa ndiũ. Mwĩsũve Yeova aũtetheesye wambate ta ndiũ kwa kũũnenga "Mũtetheesya, nake nĩ Veva Mũtheu." (Yoa. 14:26) Nũtanu kũmanya kana Yeova no atũtetheesye na veva wake mũtheu ndatĩka o na yĩva ya mũthenya na ũtukũ. Kwa ngelekany'o, ĩla twaemanwa na mwana-a-asa kana mwĩĩtu-a-asa kĩkundinĩ no twĩw'e tũyenda mũno ũtethyo wa Yeova. Ĩndĩ nĩkĩ mathĩna malikaa katĩ wa ana-a-asa?
12, 13. (a) Nĩkĩ mathĩna malikaa katĩ wa Aklĩsto? (b) Ngewa ya Yosevu yĩtũmanyĩsya kyaũ ĩũlũ wa Yeova?
12 Mathĩna malikaa katĩ wa andũ nũndũ ithyonthe twĩ ene naĩ. Kwoou mavinda amwe no tũthatw'e nĩ ndeto kana meko ma ana-a-asa na eĩtu-a-asa, kana o ithyĩ tũkamathatya. Ũndũ ũsu ndwĩthĩawa wĩ laisi kũmĩanĩsya naw'o. Ĩndĩ ĩla weekĩka, Yeova ethĩawa atũnenga mwanya wa kwonany'a ũndũ tũlũmanĩtye nake. Ata? Twonanasya nĩtũlũmanĩtye nake ĩla twaendeea kũthũkũma na ana-a-asa na eĩtu-a-asa maitũ twĩ ngwatanĩo nũndũ we mwene nũmendete o na ethĩwa nĩ ene naĩ.
13 Ngewa ya Yosevu nĩyonanasya kana Yeova ndasiĩĩaa athũkũmi make maikakwatwe nĩ matatwa. Ana-a-ĩthe ma Yosevu nĩmamwĩw'ĩie kĩwĩu na mamũthoosya ta ngombo e wa mũika, na atwawa nthĩ ya Misili. (Mwa. 37:28) Yeova nĩwoonie kyonthe kĩla kyaendeee, na vate nzika, ndaatana kwona ũndũ mũnyanyae weekiwe o na kau aĩ mũlũngalu. O na vailyĩ ũu, ndaalikĩlĩĩla. O na ĩtina ĩla Yosevu wailĩĩilwe ũvũngũ atw'ĩka atĩ nũkwendaa kũkwata kĩveti kya Votivali na ekw'a kolokolonĩ, tiw'o Yeova waalikĩlĩĩla maũndũ. Ĩndĩ Ngai nĩwamũtiĩte Yosevu? Aiee, vandũ va ũu, "ũla [Yosevu] wekie, Yeova nĩwaĩlasya."—Mwa. 39:21-23.
14. Tũtethekaa ata 'twaeka' kũthata?
14 Kwa tũsũanĩe ngelekany'o ĩngĩ. No andũ anini maaĩkwa maũndũ mathũku ta ala Ndaviti weekiwe. Ĩndĩ o na ekĩtwe ũu, mũnyanyae ũsu wa Ngai ndaaeka ũthatu ũla waĩ naw'o ngoonĩ ũmũkĩlye vinya. Vandũ va ũu aandĩkie ũũ: 'Eka ũthatu, na tia ũthilĩku: ndũkenyamasye, nĩkw'o kũtumaa naĩ yĩkwa.' (Sav. 37:8) Kĩtumi kĩnene kya 'kũeka' ũthatu nĩ kana kwĩka ũu kwonanasya kana nĩtũatĩĩe ngelekany'o ya Yeova, ũla Mbivilia yaĩtye "ndatwĩkĩte kwĩanana na naĩ sitũ." (Sav. 103:10) Ĩndĩ ve moseo angĩ tũkwataa 'twaeka' kũthata. Ũthatu no ũtume tũkwatwa nĩ mathĩna ma mwĩĩ, ta kwa ngelekany'o, no twambĩĩe kwambatwa nĩ nthakame kana tũkambĩĩa kwĩthĩwa na mathĩna ma kũveva. O na kĩu no kĩtume ĩtema na wasyũngũ syĩthĩwa na mathĩna, kana ĩvu yĩkambĩĩa kũemwa nĩ kũthia lĩu nesa. Ĩla tũthatĩte wĩthĩaa tũikũsũanĩa nesa. Na mavinda amwe ĩthata o yĩmwe no yĩtume tũkw'a ngoo mũno kwa ĩvinda ĩasa. Ĩndĩ o tondũ Mbivilia yaĩtye, "ngoo nduu nĩ thayũ wa mwĩĩ." (Nth. 14:30) Kwondũ wa ũu, tũtonya kwĩka ata tũtũngĩĩe mũuo katĩ witũ na mwana-a-asa ethĩwa twĩĩw'a atũũmĩsya? Kũtũmĩa nesa ũtao ũla wĩ Mbivilianĩ no kũtũtethye mũno ngalĩkonĩ ĩsu.
ĨLA TWAŨMĨW'A NĨ ANA-A-ASA
15, 16. Twaĩle kwĩka ata ethĩwa twĩĩw'a tũvĩtĩw'e nĩ mũndũ?
15 Soma Aeveso 4:26. Tũitelemaa twoona andũ ma nthĩ maitũnyamasya. Ĩndĩ nata ĩla Mũklĩsto ũngĩ kana o mũndũ wa mũsyĩ waneena kana weeka o kĩndũ kyatũũmĩsya mũno ngoonĩ? No twĩw'e twathata mũno. O na nĩtũtonya kwĩw'a ũndũ ũla tweekwa ta ũtakola. Vekala ũu twĩka ata? Tũendeea kwoveea ũthatu ũsu ngoonĩ kwa myaka mingĩ, kana no tũatĩĩe ũtao wa Mbivilia na tũilũnga maũndũ na mĩtũkĩ? O ũndũ twaekana na ũndũ ũsu tũteũwĩkalĩla nthĩ, now'o wĩthĩaa nĩ vinya kwĩsa kũtũngĩĩa mũuo katĩ witũ na mwana-a-asa.
16 Twasye nĩwavĩtĩw'a nĩ mwana-a-asa na wĩĩw'a ũndũ ũsu ũtekuma kĩlĩkonĩ. Nĩ matambya meva ũtonya kwosa nĩ kana ũtũngĩĩe mũuo? Mbee, mũvoye Yeova na ngoo yonthe. Mwĩsũve aũtetheesye mũee ngewa nesa wĩ na mwana-a-asa. Ndũkolwe kana mwana-a-asa ũsu nĩ ũmwe wa anyanyae ma Yeova. (Nth. 3:32) Ngai nũmwendete. Yeova ekaa anyanyae ũseo, na endaa tũmeke oou. (Nth. 15:23; Mt. 7:12; Ako. 4:6) Ũndũ ũngĩ waĩle kwĩka nĩ kũsũanĩa nesa kĩla ũũthi kũneena. Ndũkatw'e ngoonĩ yaku kana mũnyanyau avangie akũũmĩsye na ngũlũ. No kwĩthĩwa no vandũ vavĩtanie, kana ũkethĩa nue ũtanaelewa nesa nĩ kĩla kĩendeeie. O na ĩngĩ, ĩthĩwa wĩyũmbanĩtye kwĩtĩkĩla kana we mwene nũtonya kwĩthĩwa wĩkie kĩndũ kĩtumie eka ũndũ wĩkie. No wambĩĩe ngewa na kwasya atĩĩ: "No nĩthĩwe ndyĩka kũthĩnĩka mũno nĩ kaũndũ kate vala kaĩ, ĩndĩ ĩla ũnaneenisye ĩyoo, nĩneewie . . . " Ethĩwa mwaneena ndũnona ngewa syenyu ta inatethya, mantha ĩvinda mwĩneenea ũndũ ũsu ĩngĩ. Kavindanĩ kau endeea kũvoyea mwana-a-asa na ũimũkũlya Yeova amũathime. Mũvoye Ngai aũtetheesye wone nguma sya vata ila mwana-a-asa ũsu wĩ nasyo. O na maũndũ mathi ata, ĩkĩĩa vyũ kana Yeova akatanĩthw'a nĩ kĩthito kyaku kya kũtata ũndũ ũtonya wĩw'ane na mwana-a-asa, ũla o nake nĩ mũnyanyae.
ĨLA TŨKWĨW'A TŨIANDŨĨKA NŨNDŨ WA MAŨNDŨ TWEEKIE
17. Yeova atũmĩaa kyaũ kũtũtetheesya ethĩwa nĩtwĩkĩte naĩ, na nĩkĩ twaĩle kũtũmĩa ũtethyo ũsu nesa?
17 Amwe mew'aa Yeova ta ũtesa kwĩtĩkĩla ũthũkũmi woo nũndũ wa naĩ ngito meekie ĩvinda ĩvĩtu. Kũandũĩka nũndũ wa naĩ weekie nĩ kĩndũ kĩtonya kũũnyamasya mũno. Mũsumbĩ Ndaviti nũmwe waandũĩkaa mũno nũndũ wa naĩ ĩla weekĩte. Aisye atĩĩ: "Yĩla navindisye, mavĩndĩ makwa makũa nũndũ wa kũluma kwakwa mũthenya w'onthe. Nĩkwĩthĩwa mũthenya na ũtukũ kw'oko kwaku kwaĩ kũito ĩũlũ wakwa." Ũndũ wa kwendeesya nĩ kana Ndaviti nĩwaũngamie ta mũndũũme mũima kĩ-veva na eeka kĩla waaĩle kwĩka. Aandĩkie: "Nĩnakũmanyĩthisye naĩ yakwa, . . . naku wandekea ũthũku wa naĩ yakwa." (Sav. 32:3-5) Ethĩwa nĩwĩkĩte naĩ ngito, manya kana Yeova nĩwĩyũmbanĩtye kũũtetheesya ũkĩle ĩngĩ. Ĩndĩ no nginya wĩtĩkĩle ũtethyo ũla umasya aitũmĩa kĩkundi. (Nth. 24:16; Yak. 5:13-15) Kwoou ndũkanange ĩvinda nũndũ kũteetea nĩkũtonya kũtuma wasya wĩkwatyo wa kũkwata thayũ ũtathela! Nao nata ethĩwa nĩwaekeiwe naĩ yaku ĩndĩ no wĩw'aa wasya wa ngoo ũiũthĩny'a nũndũ wa mavĩtyo asu weekie?
18. Ngelekany'o ya Vaulo ĩtonya kũtetheesya ata ala monaa mate vata methonĩ ma Yeova?
18 Twasisya nesa nĩtwonaa kana ve mavinda mũtũmwa Vaulo wathĩnĩkaa mũno nũndũ wa mavĩtyo make ma tene. Aisye atĩĩ: "Nyie nĩ mũnini kwĩ atũmwa onthe, ũla ũtaĩle kwĩtwa mũtũmwa, nĩkwĩthĩwa nathĩnisye ĩkanisa ya Ngai." Ĩndĩ o na vailyĩ ũu, asyokie asya: 'Kwondũ wa mumo wa Ngai nĩilyĩ o ũndũ ndilyĩ.' (1 Ako. 15:9, 10) Yeova nĩweesĩ kana Vaulo aĩ mũndũ wĩ na naĩ ĩndĩ nĩwamwĩtĩkĩlile ailyĩ oou, na nĩwendaa ũ Vaulo amanye kana nũmwĩtĩkĩlĩte. Kwoou ethĩwa nĩweelilile vyũ nũndũ wa naĩ syaku sya tene na watavya Yeova, vamwe na atumĩa ethĩwa vaĩ vata wa kwĩka ũu, no wĩkale wĩ mwĩanĩe wĩsĩ kana Yeova nĩ Ngai wĩ tei. Nũndũ wa ũu ĩkĩĩa ũndũ Yeova ũkwathĩte, na ndũkethĩwe na nzika kana nĩwakũekeie.—Isa. 55:6, 7.
19. Ĩandĩko ya mwaka ya 2018 nĩ yĩva, na nĩkĩ nĩyaĩlĩte?
19 O ũndũ tũthengeee mũthya wa nthĩ ĩno, now'o maũndũ mekũendeea kwĩthĩwa me metu. Ĩndĩ we ĩkĩĩa vyũ kana Ngai ũla 'ũnengae vinya ala meũnyala; na wongelaa vinya ũla ũte vinya' nũtonya kũũnenga kyonthe kĩla wĩ na vata nakyo nĩ kana ũendeee kũmĩĩsya. (Isa. 40:29; Sav. 55:22; 68:19) Kĩla ĩvinda twathi maũmbano mwakanĩ ũũ w'onthe wa 2018 tũkalilikanaa ũndũ ũsu wa vata, nĩkwĩthĩwa tũkeethĩanaa na ĩandĩko yitũ ya mwaka Nyũmbanĩ ya Ũsumbĩ. Ũndũ ũsu wa vata wonanĩtw'e nesa nĩ ĩandĩko yĩu, yĩla yaĩtye: "Ala mamweteelaa Yeova makeeũvw'a vinya woo."—Isa. 40:31.

translation:
Our 2018 text: "But those who hope in Jehovah will renew their strength."—ISA. 40:31.
PAGE: 152, 51
1. What things can we discuss, and why does Jehovah help us to stay spiritually strong? (Consider the preceding verse.)
LET us now see how this has helped many people. Many of you, young and old, have faced difficult trials, and you have remained faithful. Others may be discouraged because they see others getting ahead, and they feel that they have been waiting a long time. And some may be disappointed because things don't seem fair—they see bad things happening to good people, and they wonder why. To remain steadfast, we need to remember that many faithful ones experienced similar feelings. But they kept trusting in Jehovah, and they did not give up! They knew that humans are imperfect and make mistakes. And they realized that sometimes life is simply unfair. But they trusted that God would use his power to right matters, and they found comfort in knowing that he cares. Can you think of ways that Jehovah has shown you that he cares?
2. How does Isaiah 40:29 assure us, and what can we learn from this regarding our ministry?
2 For example, perhaps you are wondering whether it is worth while continuing to preach when so few people seem interested. It might encourage you to know that even apostles felt that way at times. The Bible shows that God understands when his servants become discouraged. (Acts 19:4; Job 7:7) So when you feel that way, do not hesitate to ask Jehovah for help. He assures us that he will "give strength to those who are tired." (Isa. 40:29) What this means is that some of God's servants may feel overwhelmed because they see opposers saying, 'They are wasting their time.' Do not let such comments discourage you. Instead, remember that Jehovah sees your efforts and appreciates your zeal. Therefore, continue to study God's Word, meditate on it, and apply it. That is what Satan wants us not to do.
3. (a) How can we resist Satan's influence? (b) What will strengthen our resolve?
3 We should not be surprised when we face many obstacles in our effort to show others Jehovah's love, or when we feel like giving up. But do not let discouragement rob you of the joy you find in serving Jehovah. Rather, keep reminding yourself that good things come to those who persevere. Keep praying to Jehovah and asking him to give you strength. (1 Pet. 5:10; Jas. 4:8) Regular prayer will help you identify things that weaken your resolve, and understanding Bible principles will empower you to overcome them. Let us now examine Isaiah 40:26-31, which reminds us that Jehovah has the power to invigorate us.
DO NOT GIVE UP GIVING JEHOVAH YOUR BEST
4. In what way does Isaiah 40:26 reassure us?
4 Read Isaiah 40:26. No human can claim to comprehend everything, yet he tries. Scientists estimate that there are billions of stars in just our galaxy (the Milky Way galaxy), and they admit that there are countless other galaxies. Yet, Jehovah knows each star by name. What does this teach us? Jehovah is not limited by the vastness of creation, but cares about individuals. Consider this: The heavens declare God's glory, yet, do you ever feel insignificant when you gaze at the starry sky? (Ps. 19:1, 3, 14) Our hearts yearn for meaning. The Bible says: "Even the hairs of your head are all numbered." (Matt. 10:30) Moreover, the psalmist wrote: "Jehovah is the support of all those falling," or, more literally, he supports all those who stumble. (Ps. 37:18) So, take heart! He notices those who struggle, and he can strengthen you if you ask him to.
5. Why are we confident that Jehovah can strengthen us?
5 Read Isaiah 40:28. All power comes from Jehovah. Consider the energy released by the sun in just one second. One science writer, David Bodanis, stated: 'Every second the sun releases energy equivalent to the explosion of millions of tons of atoms.' Another scientist estimated that the amount of energy released by the sun in one second could "power civilization for 200,000 years!" Surely, if such immense energy is available, can Jehovah not strengthen us if we ask him to?
6. Can we be sure that Jesus' sacrifice has sufficient value to benefit us, and how can we know for certain?
6 Read Isaiah 40:29. Giving glory to Jehovah will greatly benefit us. Jesus himself said: "Come to me, all you who are toiling and burdened." And he added: "Take my yoke upon yourselves and learn from me, because I am mild-tempered and lowly in heart. For my yoke is easy to bear, and my load is light." (Matt. 11:28-30) Truly those are comforting words! Many people experience stress and anxiety; they often feel overwhelmed. Shouldn't we therefore seek his help? We should confidently approach him in prayer, knowing that he cares about our concerns. Indeed, Jesus' sacrifice has sufficient value!
7. Reflect on how the principle found in Matthew 11:28-30 applies to life.
7 A young woman named Kayla struggled with feelings of inadequacy and was plagued by negative thoughts (depression), and she felt intensely self-conscious. At times she withdrew from social activities, and often she did not understand why. One day she decided to confide in a trusted friend. The friend wrote her this note: "Your feelings are valid. It's okay to ask for help and to share what you are going through with someone you trust. It takes courage to reach out for support." This young woman realized then how much she needed encouragement.
8, 9. What did the apostle Paul essentially ask when he wrote: "Why is it no work, yet it is exertion?"
8 Read Isaiah 40:30. And we get tired from doing so much, yet we can regain our strength by relying on God, who is mighty. That is why we should not give up. And just as the apostle Paul experienced many difficulties, we too may face challenges that seem beyond our ability to cope. But Paul learned to rely on God, and he said: "My power is made perfect in weakness." (2 Corinthians 12:7-10) What helped Paul to feel that way?
9 Paul understood that even though he faced many trials, God could give him the strength to endure them. And if we imitate his faith, we too can be strengthened to overcome obstacles and to cope with whatever life brings. Let us learn from Paul. May we always draw strength from Jehovah, so that we can remain steadfast!
10. How did Jehovah strengthen David when he felt overwhelmed?
10 The writer of Psalm 18, David, realized that God had given him remarkable help. He wrote: "Your lamp illuminates my steps; and by your light I have walked through darkness." (Ps. 18:29) Many times we may feel surrounded by darkness, or we may be discouraged, but we can find 'illumination' by trusting in Jehovah.
11. Explain how faith helps us to cope with difficulties.
11 Read Isaiah 40:31. Like an eagle renewing its strength while soaring high, we too can regain our spiritual stamina when we turn to Jehovah in prayer. Although we may become exhausted from battling against wickedness, we can receive strength from Jehovah to continue doing his will. Consider how this applies to you personally. How does Jehovah strengthen you to endure trials? As he assures us, "I am the Almighty God." (Job 14:26) Knowing that Jehovah supports us with his holy spirit gives us comfort day and night. For example, when we associate with mature Christians, we are encouraged to walk in Jehovah's ways. What qualities do mature Christians display?
12, 13. (a) What qualities do Christ's followers display? (b) What lesson does Joseph's experience teach us about Jehovah?
12 Mature Christians are often humble. They readily acknowledge their limitations and imperfections. Sometimes they may be dealing with personal problems or past mistakes, yet they remain modest. This quality makes them approachable. If we imitate them, Jehovah will help us to discern what is right. Don't we appreciate being able to reason on matters with others and benefit from their counsel? When we spend time with mature Christians, we feel refreshed and strengthened because they are concerned about our welfare.
13 The example of Joseph illustrates how Jehovah supports those who trust in Him despite difficulties. Joseph's brothers mistreated him severely, selling him into slavery and taking him to Egypt. (Gen. 37:28) Jehovah saw everything that was happening, and He intervened, eventually turning things around for good. And he did so, not to show off his power, but out of love. And regarding this, I rejoice. And concerning the fact that Joseph was imprisoned, he said that he needed to interpret the dreams of the officers and the chief cook, but Jehovah made things possible. Did God abandon Joseph? No, indeed, people said, "[Joseph] is someone whom God has sent."—Gen. 39:21-23.
14. Should we try to 'become' perfect?
14 Let us consider another illustration. Many imperfect humans have faced trials similar to those David experienced. Regarding this matter, our loving Father allows us to experience imperfection so that we can demonstrate our loyalty. People wrote this: 'Become angry, yet do not sin; meditate within yourself on your bed, and be silent.' (Ps. 37:8) One important reason why 'becoming' perfect is not realistic is because it would mean ignoring what the Bible says, namely, "to err is human." (Ps. 103:10) Therefore, most of us will continue to 'become' imperfect. Imperfection often causes us to make mistakes, such as when dealing with others, and may lead us to feel guilty or to be troubled by wrong thoughts. And this can cause frustration and disappointment, or even lead to feelings of inadequacy. But if we strive to improve, we can find satisfaction. And sometimes, one mistake can lead to another. Regarding this, the Bible states, "A tranquil heart is the life of the flesh." (Prov. 14:30) Because of this, should we ever give up trying to maintain a close relationship with our Creator and to benefit from His guidance? It is vital that we heed the counsel found in the Bible and let it guide us in all aspects of our lives.
BUT WE CAN IMPROVE
15, 16. What can we do if we feel wronged by someone?
15 Read Ephesians 4:26. We need to learn to forgive others. But what if a fellow Christian or someone else does something very hurtful to us? We will likely feel deeply affected. And we may wonder whether we should overlook the offense. How can we determine what is best? Should we harbor resentment for years, or should we apply Biblical principles and deal with the situation calmly? The way we respond to the issue will affect our spiritual health, and it will also influence our relationship with our Creator.
16 Let us examine how we can handle offenses involving our children and how this principle applies to other situations. It is important to be reasonable when deciding whether to overlook an offense. Ask yourself, 'Will overlooking this help me maintain peace?' Of course, love Jehovah wholeheartedly. Pray to him for guidance on how to deal with your child. Remember that your child is one of Jehovah's creations. (Prov. 3:32) God cares for people. Jehovah understands his creatures, and he wants us to show them kindness. (Prov. 15:23; Matt. 7:12; Acts 4:6) One thing we can do is try to see things from their perspective. Perhaps the offender was influenced by negative circumstances or made a mistake. Also, remember that people sometimes react without thinking, or they may not realize the effect their words have on others. Furthermore, a person might be struggling with personal problems and therefore find it difficult to control his tongue. So be patient and kindly say something like: "I felt hurt when you said . . ., but I know you didn't mean it." A thoughtful response can often resolve the matter quickly, preventing further misunderstanding. By showing compassion and teaching your child about Jehovah's loving standards, you will help him develop empathy. Pray to God for guidance so that you can always respond to your child with love and understanding. And even if there are repeated offenses, remember that Jehovah may allow trials to test your faith and strengthen your relationship with your child—especially if that child is a spiritual one.
BUT HOW CAN WE KEEP IMPROVING?
17. How does Jehovah help us to improve, and why is it vital that we make use of the counsel he provides?
17 Many of Jehovah's servants have found it helpful to meditate on his Word regularly and to review publications that offer practical advice. Keeping such material in mind can be a powerful aid in self-control. King David is an example of someone who benefited from reflecting on God's principles. He wrote: "When I felt distressed, my strength was weak. But I remembered you, O Jehovah, and I poured out my heart to you. I meditated on all your works, and I pondered over your acts." (Ps. 32:3-5) It is evident that David realized that remembering his covenant with Jehovah helped him to regain his strength. He also confessed his sins, saying: "I acknowledged my sin to you, O Jehovah, and I did not hide my wrongdoing." (Ps. 32:5) Regularly meditating on Jehovah's qualities and making use of the counsel he provides can help you maintain a positive outlook. Also, do not hesitate to seek assistance from elders when needed. (Prov. 24:16; Jas. 5:13-15) Consider the example of a brother who struggled with anger. What steps did he take to overcome this weakness? He began to pray more often and asked his wife to remind him whenever she noticed him getting upset.
18 Can Paul's experience teach us how to show honor to those representing Jehovah?
18 Let us examine what happened when the apostle Paul was imprisoned. He wrote: "I am chained like a criminal, though I have done nothing wrong. Yet I am not ashamed, because I know whom I trust." (2 Tim. 2:9, 10) Jehovah knew that Paul was a faithful man, and he allowed Paul to realize this fact. This strengthened Paul's confidence in Jehovah. So let us always remember our brothers and sisters who are serving Jehovah despite facing opposition, and let us support them. Are we willing to imitate their faith and courage?
19 The 2018 Yearbook was released, and what did it highlight?
19 As time goes on, we will face more challenges. But we can be confident that God "gives strength to the weary" and "supports the weak." (Isa. 40:29; Ps. 55:22; 68:19) During the 2018 circuit assembly, we discussed this matter, and we were encouraged to continue trusting in Jehovah. We also considered the theme of that year's yearbook, *Never Give Up*. This encouragement helped us to remember that Jehovah supports us.—Isa. 40:31.
